[Chrono initialization](https://arxiv.org/abs/1804.11188) provides a way to encourage multiple memory timescales using existing GRU gates. For the convention hₜ=zₜhₜ₋₁+(1−zₜ)h̃ₜ, a desired constant retention r implies bias logit(r) and direct-path e-folding horizon τ=−1/log(r). These are nominal initialization horizons: inputs, gate derivatives and candidate-state recurrence change actual persistence. [GRU Jacobian analysis](https://proceedings.mlr.press/v107/can20a.html) shows update gates can create slow modes, while reset gates influence spectral radius; gate biases alone cannot establish effective memory.

Recent evidence supports testing initialization without adding gates. A [2026 controlled synthetic-task study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.29034) reports all 360 chrono-initialized runs reached its validation criterion, with substantial tolerance to misspecified horizons. This does not establish recommendation gains or the superiority of heterogeneous horizons. [Zucchet and Orvieto, NeurIPS 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.21064), additionally show that longer memory can increase sensitivity to parameter changes even without exploding gradients. Longer retention therefore need not improve optimization or accuracy.

Suggested experiment, inferred from these findings: compare baseline, heterogeneous retention biases and a uniform control matching mean initial retention, keeping architecture and training fixed. Matching mean retention controls one-step carry, not the entire decay curve. Measure trained gate distributions alongside finite-horizon Jacobian-product gains and small hidden-state perturbation decay under identical subsequent inputs; exclude padding steps. Add history-truncation or prefix-perturbation effects on recommendation scores to assess task relevance. Select using macro validation HR@10. Existing temporal results alone do not establish excessive memory; distinguish nominal carry, actual state persistence and useful predictive dependence.
